8.0.s.en: (3) The thirst of the people and their demand to surrender the city

8.0.0.en: The Holy Bible presents us here with the person of Judith – the meaning of which is "Jewess" – and tells us of her lineage. She was from the tribe of Simeon, as is confirmed at the beginning of the ninth chapter (ch. 9:2-3). She speaks of her father Simeon, of whom his father Jacob said that he was wrathful, and in his anger he and Levi rose up because of Shechem's assault on their sister, and they rose and killed all the men of the city (Gen 49:5-7). She is proud of belonging to Simeon, who was distinguished for courage, and she does not mean his rashness and impetuosity, for Judith was courageous like her ancestor Simeon. As for the mention of Reuben, it may be because he was considered the firstborn of Jacob; and in the Jesuit translation of this book the name of Reuben is not mentioned.

8.0.1.en: It is to be noted that Judith's descent is traced back to her ancestor Simeon and includes fifteen generations, because the Jews – until the birth of Christ – took care of their genealogies, so that God might declare the fulfillment of His promise that Christ would come from the seed of David and from the seed of Judah.

8.0.2.en: Among the graces of God is that this great woman – as will become clear from what follows – did not live beside the temple in Jerusalem, but in the northern kingdom of the Jews, whose capital is Samaria, where the worship of idols was widespread, and yet she remained holding fast to her faith; indeed her faith was very strong, as appears also in the person of the great Tobit in his love and his faith, who was also from the northern kingdom. For God is able to keep you and to develop your faith however bad the circumstances around you, if you continue to hold fast to Him.

8.1.0.en: Urged on: encourages and motivates the workers to work energetically.

8.1.1.en: Struck: that is, scorched; the meaning is that his temperature rose as a result of the intense heat of the sun on his head.

8.1.2.en: Judith married and her husband died – as it seems – at a young age, a short time after her marriage, for Manasseh her husband was working energetically in the field during the harvest, making light of the fatigue because he was young, and the intense heat struck him and he died. As a rich man and an owner of possessions he used to urge on the workers in his fields to complete the harvest, and the sun struck him, because the barley harvest is in about the month of May and the heat then is intense.

8.1.3.en: Sunstroke in ancient times was difficult to treat and ended a person's life, as happened with the son of the Shunammite woman, the widow, whom Elisha the prophet raised (2 Kgs 4:18-20).

8.2.0.en: After the death of Judith's husband she kept to her widowhood, although she was young and very beautiful and rich, and this is a proof of her chastity.

8.2.1.en: Her husband died and she accepted the affliction as an opportunity to live with God. She represents the human soul that accepts God's dispensations with thanksgiving, and even seizes affliction to draw near to God and consecrate her heart to Him.

8.2.2.en: The period of three and a half years is that in which Elijah shut up heaven, that the people might repent and return to God, and after this the heavy rain came down (Jas 5). It also signifies the period of affliction at the end of the days, of which the Book of Revelation tells us (Rev 12), which the children of God endure, or the three and a half days in which the bodies of the two prophets lie in the street of the great city, and then rise (Rev 11), of which Daniel prophesied (Dan 12). So after a widowhood of three and a half years, Judith rejoiced in the salvation of God by her hands for all her people, and Holofernes, who signifies Satan, died, and all his soldiers were defeated. For the period of three and a half years signifies the temporary afflictions that we endure in life, after which the crisis is relieved.

8.2.3.en: Judith did not need to marry her husband's brother – as the Law requires – because she desired virginity, and God helped her in that by widowhood. So she lived all her life worshiping God in chastity and asceticism, like Anna the prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel (Lk 2:36-38).

8.2.4.en: Truly all things work together for good to them that love God (Rom 8:28). God manages your life even if you do not understand; He permits affliction so that He may be glorified in it and work in weakness more than in human strength, as the Apostle Paul said, "When I am weak, then am I strong" (2 Cor 12:10).

8.3.0.en: Her loins: the middle and below, the region of the body that the undergarments cover.

8.3.1.en: Sackcloth: a coarse garment resembling burlap.

8.3.2.en: New moons: the Jews used to keep a feast at the beginning of the months.

8.3.3.en: Household: the private servants and maidservants whom she owned.

8.3.4.en: The Holy Bible testifies that Judith was very rich, and even describes her many possessions of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep, and yet she left behind all these many comforts and left behind what every woman cares about, namely her beauty, although she possessed wonderful beauty. And strangely, she also gave up the enjoyment of her great mansion and lived in an upper room, to live a life of solitude in many prayers and acts of worship.

8.3.5.en: Thus she lived voluntary poverty, and she is a clear example from the Old Testament of the importance of solitude and seclusion, which appeared as the system of monasticism in the New Testament.

8.3.6.en: It is worth pointing out the good influence of Judith on her maidservants who worked in her house, for they too came to love prayer and worship, so her upper room became a house for virgins. Perhaps St. Demiana and the forty virgins followed her example when they lived in the palace that Marcus the governor built for his daughter Demiana. She was distinguished in her solitude by severe asceticism, for she left behind the soft garments of the rich and put on sackcloth, that is, coarse garments, as an application of severe austerity, and she fasted all the year, except the festal days of the liturgical calendar that the Law prescribes.

8.3.7.en: And when Judith fled from the delights of the world and its fame, honor ran after her, so all the people of Bethulia felt her piety, and everyone esteemed her and honored her.

8.3.8.en: And you, what have you given up of material things and lust for the sake of God? How great is your effort to be alone with God and to enjoy prayers and meditations? And how many souls have been influenced by you and drawn by you to the love of Christ?

8.3.9.en: (2) The rebuke of the elders of the city (vv. 9-13:)

8.3.10.en: 9- Now when she heard that Ozias had promised to surrender the city after five days, she sent to the two elders Chabris and Karmi. 10- And they came to her, and she said to them, What is this thing which Ozias has agreed to, to surrender the city to the Assyrians if no help comes to us within five days? 11- Who are you that tempt the Lord? 12- This is not a word that obtains mercy, but rather stirs up wrath and kindles anger. 13- For you have set a term for the mercy of the Lord, and appointed him a day as it pleases you.

8.4.1.en: Judith sent to the chief elders of the city, the two elders Chabris and Karmi, who were perhaps the assistants of Ozias the head, or elder, of the city. She sent to them because she did not want to leave her solitude and walk in the streets of the city, and she did not summon Ozias the head of the city, either out of respect and regard for his position, or because she did not want to hinder him from leading the multitudes of the agitated and grieving people, so she called his assistants only.

8.5.0.en: They came: they arrived at her house.

8.5.1.en: The two elders responded to Judith's call, because of her great spiritual standing in the city. When the two elders came, she rebuked them with all boldness and gentleness for what Ozias had declared and the elders had agreed to, since they yielded to the pressure of the people, when Ozias asked them to give God a respite of five days, and if He did not rescue them, they would surrender the city to the Assyrians.

8.5.2.en: And this opinion, although it was better than the opinion of the people, who wanted to surrender the city at once, was nevertheless a great error in the eyes of Judith, who, it seems, had a spiritual stature higher than all the rest.

8.6.2.en: A term: a period or the end of an appointed time.

8.6.3.en: Judith made clear the error of what Ozias had declared in two matters:

8.6.4.en: 1- This is weakness of faith and doubt in God, indeed a tempting of Him, for Ozias gives God a respite to complete His work at an appointed time, otherwise he will surrender the city to the Assyrians, and this is not fitting at all.

8.6.5.en: For God is able to do all things and He should be waited for without limit, for we have none other than Him.

8.6.6.en: 2- It is not proper, or humble, to place conditions on God that He may rescue us, but seeking His mercy is by submitting to Him and delivering our life completely, and He rescues us at the time He Himself sees, for He loves us and knows our good better than we do. She warned them that fixing a respite for God to work in provokes His wrath against them, because fixing a period means tempting God, and this greatly grieves God, as in (Ex 17:2-7, Mt 4:7). There is a difference between persistence and fixing a period for the work of God, because persistence and asking for God's quick intervention means faith, clinging to God, and waiting for His intervention with constant importunity toward Him. This is, of course, not the same as fixing a period, and if God does not act within it, leaving Him and looking for other solutions.

8.6.7.en: I wish that you would rely on God with complete faith and be confident that He does not forget you, even if afflictions increase upon you and despair fights you. Be strong and continue your prayers, to overcome evil thoughts, and you will always enjoy the mercies of God. (3) Their call to repentance (vv. 14-29:)

8.6.8.en: 14- But since the Lord is long-suffering, let us repent of this and seek His forgiveness with tears poured out.

8.6.9.en: 15- For the threat of God is not like the threat of man, neither does He burn with anger like the son of man. 16- Therefore let us humble our souls before Him and serve Him in a humble spirit. 17- And let us ask the Lord with tears to grant us His mercy according to His will, that we may glory in our humility, just as our hearts were troubled by their pride. 18- For we have not walked in the sins of our fathers, who left their God and worshiped strange gods. 19- For which iniquity they were delivered to the sword and to spoil and to shame among their enemies, but we know no other god than Him. 20- So let us hope in humility for His comfort, and He will avenge our blood on the oppression of our enemies against us, and will bring down all the nations that rise up against us, and the Lord our God will put them to shame. 21- And now, O brethren, since you are elders in the people of God and their souls depend on you, raise up their hearts by your words, that they may remember that it was only to prove our fathers whether they would truly worship their God that trial came upon them. 22- They should therefore remember how our father Abraham was tried, and after being proved by many tribulations became the friend of God. 23- And so Isaac, and so Jacob, and so Moses, and all those with whom God was pleased passed through many tribulations and remained faithful. 24- But those who did not receive the trials with the fear of the Lord, but showed their impatience, and their murmuring against the Lord returned upon them, 25- were destroyed by the destroyer and perished by serpents.

8.6.10.en: 26- But as for us now, let us not be impatient at what we suffer. 27- But let us esteem these punishments to be less than our sins, and believe that the scourges of the Lord, with which we are chastened like servants, are for amendment and not for destruction. 28- Then Ozias and the elders said to her, All that you have said is true, and there is no fault in your words. 29- Now therefore pray for us, for you are a holy woman and fear God.

8.7.0.en: Burns: is kindled and his anger intensifies.

8.7.1.en: With anger: with rage and severe wrath.

8.7.2.en: Judith reassured the two elders that God is not like men, impetuous in His wrath or vengeance, and that He will not hasten to chastise the people for what they had resolved to do, so there is still an opportunity for repentance. She advised them to humble themselves before God with humility, tears, prayers and contrite worship together with the people, and God would forgive them for what they had said, and have mercy on them, and rescue them from the Assyrians as He sees fit and at the time He appoints, for His will is good, so they would triumph by this over their enemies and glory in this humility that brought upon them the mercies of God, instead of the turmoil that shook their hearts because of the pride and might of their enemies.

8.7.3.en: Humility is your way to win all the battles against the devil and to enjoy the fullness of the work of the divine power in you.

8.8.0.en: We have walked: we have followed.

8.8.1.en: What reassures and encourages us is that we have not left our God and worshiped strange gods, but worship God alone; for when our fathers became proud and worshiped strange gods, God left them, and they were exposed to the aggression of the enemies around them with killing and plunder, so they fell into great shame, as happened in the days of the Judges and the wicked kings, when their neighbors attacked them and humbled them.

8.9.0.en: Oppression: that is, harshness, which means injustice and tyranny.

8.9.1.en: Those who rise up against us: those who leap upon us, that is, those who attack us.

8.9.2.en: By our faith in God and our humility before Him we ask for His mercies, and He rescues us from our enemies who wrong us, and puts them to shame, humbles them and takes vengeance on them, and so saves our souls.

8.9.3.en: Let us stand firm in the faith, and draw near to God in humility, hoping in Him at all times, and He will remove evils from us.

8.10.2.en: Judith continued her speech with the two elders. It seems that the news of her summoning the two elders had reached the head of the city, Ozias, and out of his regard for this great lady Judith, he felt the importance of the matter, and hurried in humility himself to her house to learn what she wanted in this severe trial through which their city Bethulia was passing. Perhaps he took it as an opportunity to receive a blessing from this pious woman, and he joined the two elders to listen to the guidance and teachings of this saint who by her piety and wisdom led her people in the way of God and brought about victory for it.

8.10.3.en: She said to them that since they were responsible for the souls of this people, they must alert them to an important spiritual principle, which is that God permits afflictions to test His children, and if they obey Him and hold fast to Him, they are proved and receive a great blessing.

8.10.4.en: It is to be noted that Judith did not speak to the people directly, out of her regard for the position and function of the elders responsible for teaching the people, who signify the role of the priests and deacons in the New Testament. It is not fitting for a woman to teach the people, except for teaching women and children.

8.11.0.en: And she gave them examples, such as our father Abraham, whom God tested by his leaving his city and going out into the wilderness (Gen 32:1) and his offering Isaac his son as a sacrifice (Gen 22), so his faith was proved and he became the father of all the Jewish people, and God's promises were fulfilled in him. Also the holy fathers Isaac (Gen 22, 25:21) and Jacob (Gen 29-31) and Moses (Gen 34:1-4) and all who pleased the Lord and endured afflictions steadfast in their faith.

8.12.0.en: The destroyer destroyed them: God exterminated them.

8.12.1.en: As for those who refused faith by murmuring, such as the people of Israel, who murmured in the wilderness of Sinai, after their going out from the land of Egypt, several times: for example, when they murmured against the manna, their heavenly food, and craved the meat and the onions and the leeks which were in the land of Egypt; or when they murmured at the scarcity of water; or when they were afraid to enter the promised land because of the inhabitants of the land, so they were prevented from entering it and those who were afraid died in the wilderness; and when they murmured against the manna and the quail, the serpents bit them.

8.12.2.en: So affliction is a blessing that God permits, so let us not murmur at it, lest we lose its blessings and God forsake us and we be exposed to greater afflictions and God be angry with us.

8.13.1.en: Less than our sins: less than our sins deserve.

8.13.2.en: Then Judith summarized how the people of Bethulia should conduct themselves in the face of this great affliction, as follows:

8.13.3.en: 1- Not to be troubled by the difficulty of the affliction, but to stand firm in the faith and be reassured of God's care and His protection of us.

8.13.4.en: 2- To look at our sins, that is, to examine ourselves and repent, and then we feel that we deserve afflictions far greater than this affliction because of the multitude of our sins; that is, the affliction leads us to deep repentance.

8.13.5.en: 3- To be confident, despite the difficulty of the affliction, which shows our weakness as weak servants and not great masters, that it turns to our good and mends many of our faults and brings us near to God.

8.13.6.en: I wish that you would meditate on the blessings of the afflictions that have passed through your life and thank God for them, so that this is a safeguard for you against any turmoil that attacks you if a new affliction comes upon you.

8.14.0.en: How great was the humility of Ozias, and of the elders Chabris and Karmi, before Judith. And how strong is the awe and influence of the words of the saints on those who listen to them. They felt their error in what they had declared to the people, and agreed with Judith in what she guided them to in her beautiful spiritual sermon.

8.14.1.en: They also felt that they were before a great saint, so they asked her to pray for them and for all the people.

8.14.2.en: In proportion to how much you live with God in holy worship and enjoy fellowship with Him in prayers and meditations, to that extent will be your spiritual influence on those around you, and your service will be successful, and you will win many souls.

8.14.4.en: 30- Then Judith said to them, As you have known that what I have spoken is from God, 31- so know about what I have resolved that it is from God, and pray that God may confirm my counsel. 32- This night you shall stand at the gate, and I will go out with my maidservant, and pray that the Lord may look upon His people Israel in the five days as you have said. 33- And I do not wish that you inquire into my purpose, and from now until I tell you of it, do nothing but pray to the Lord our God for us. 34- Then Ozias said to her, Judah commands you, go in peace, and may the Lord be with you in taking vengeance on our enemies. And they departed, returning

8.15.0.en: Judith ended her speech with the elders, that since they had trusted in her faith and her teaching, which they had agreed to, she asked them to trust in what she would do, for with her experience and fellowship with God she was confident that her conduct was sound, and she asked for their prayers that God would complete His work with her for the rescue of His people.

8.16.0.en: Then Judith asked the elders to stand at the gate of the city that night, to bid her farewell and bless her as she went out with her maidservant to meet the enemies, and she repeated her request that they pray for her, that God might rescue His people during the coming five days.

8.16.1.en: Despite her refusal to fix a period for the work of God, she was confident that God in His love would condescend and rescue them before the expiry of this respite, out of compassion for His people, making allowance for them in the weakness of their faith.

8.17.0.en: And she asked two things of them:

8.17.1.en: 1- Not to ask about the nature of her mission and its details.

8.17.2.en: 2- To pray for her, that God might complete the rescue of His people by her hands.

8.17.3.en: Judith bore alone the responsibility of rescuing her people, and told no one the details of her mission, because she had compassion on those around her, lest their faith in God's help for her be shaken, in addition to the fact that their compassion for her might lead them to prevent her from carrying out her mission.

8.17.4.en: When you find those around you in weakness, instead of blaming them for their weakness, bear the responsibility in their place, and help them and rescue them by the power of God from their troubles.

8.18.0.en: When the elders heard this surprise, that is, Judith's secret mission, they submitted to her words, and Ozias, the head of the city, spoke in their name. The Holy Bible calls him here "the prince of Judah," considering that the temple of God in Jerusalem belongs to the tribe of Judah, and the city of Bethulia believes in the God who dwells in the temple in Jerusalem, so their head is called prince of Judah... And he told her to go in the peace of God to complete her mission, raising prayers for her, that God might help her and rescue His people by her hands.

8.18.1.en: The three elders departed from her house, and perhaps they went to the synagogue, or to one of the houses, and gathered to pray for Judith, then went to wait for her at the gate of the city, and stood there in prayer waiting for her to go out that night, as she had told them, to complete her mission. Their feelings were all reverence and awe, because of the difficulty of her mission and compassion for her because of the difficulty of the situation, and at the same time confidence in her holiness and the power of God supporting her was stirring in their hearts, while the sense of the people's humiliation through thirst and their nearness to death tormented them, as they besought God for His quick answer and His compassion on them. It was the sense of responsibility together with the sense of weakness before the difficulty of the situation; so they humbled themselves before God, waiting for His salvation.

8.18.2.en: The prayer of Judith before she left the city
